hints: Start by reminding yourself what an ideal gas is assumed to do, with particles that have no attraction for each other.
Recall that real gases get closest to ideal at low pressure and high temperature, when particles are far apart and moving fast.
Ask yourself which choice directly reduces attraction between particles so they behave more like independent, point-like particles.
walkthrough:
**Recall the ideal gas assumptions**

Think of an ideal gas as particles with zero volume and zero attraction. They just fly, collide elastically, and keep going.

Ideal model assumes:
$$\text{intermolecular forces} = 0 \text{ and particle volume} \approx 0$$

**See when real gases match this**

Real gases deviate when particles are squeezed close together or moving slowly, so attractions matter. That is why low pressure (particles far apart) and high temperature (particles have high kinetic energy to overcome attractions) help.

**Link polarity and forces to ideality**

Polar molecules have stronger dipole attractions, so they deviate more. Weaker intermolecular forces means less attraction, so the gas naturally behaves more like the ideal assumption of no attraction.

options.A: Higher pressure squeezes particles closer together. This makes particle volume significant and intermolecular forces more important, so deviation from ideal increases, not decreases.
options.B: Lower temperature means lower kinetic energy. Particles move slowly and are more easily held by intermolecular forces, even allowing liquefaction, so behaviour becomes less ideal.
options.C: More polar molecules have stronger permanent dipole-dipole forces. Stronger attractions break the ideal assumption of no intermolecular forces, so deviation increases.
options.D: Weaker intermolecular forces means attractions are closer to zero. This directly matches the ideal gas assumption, so the gas is much more likely to obey $pV = nRT$.
